name: Uriah the Hittite
charge: Refusing the comfort of his own house while the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents
summary: Recalled from the siege of Rabbah so that the king's crime could be covered, he would not go down to his house. He slept at the door of the king's house with the servants. Asked why, he said the ark and Israel and Judah abide in tents, and my lord Joab and the servants of my lord are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house? He was made drunk and still would not go, and was sent back carrying the letter that ordered his death.
offense: Uriah the Hittite is numbered among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39). When recalled from the war, he would not receive the comforts of his own house while the ark, Israel, Judah, Joab, and the servants remained in tents and the open fields. He answered David with an oath that he would not do such a thing (2 Samuel 11:11). David's invitation would have been convenient to accept. Uriah had the king's permission to go home, and the king sent a mess of meat after him. Yet he slept at the door of the king's house with the servants (2 Samuel 11:8-9). His concern reached beyond what he was personally allowed to enjoy. He remembered the men still bearing the burden from which he had briefly been recalled. Even when David made him drunk, Uriah did not return to his wife (2 Samuel 11:13). The purpose concealed behind the hospitality failed. The servant maintained his course while the king employed his authority to hide a transgression. David then entrusted him with the letter that ordered his death. Uriah carried it to Joab and returned to the fighting (2 Samuel 11:14-17). The loyalty by which he served his king was used against him. His death did not expose a failure of courage or duty; it exposed the treachery of the command placed over him. Nathan's charge did not let Uriah disappear into the unnamed losses of battle. The Lord declared that David had killed Uriah with the sword and taken his wife (2 Samuel 12:9). The man whom the king had sought to conceal remained named in the judgment against the king. The later summary of David's reign again singled out the matter of Uriah the Hittite (1 Kings 15:5). Matthew also identifies Solomon's mother as her who had been the wife of Urias (Matthew 1:6). The record of the royal line did not erase the marriage that David had violated. Uriah was not delivered from the fatal order. His fidelity must not be measured by whether he escaped suffering. The account honours the servant's conduct while condemning the ruler who exploited it. The throne could command his movements, but it could not make the blood innocent of accusation.
offenseFull: Uriah the Hittite is numbered among David's mighty men (2 Samuel 23:39). When recalled from the war, he would not receive the comforts of his own house while the ark, Israel, Judah, Joab, and the servants remained in tents and the open fields. He answered David with an oath that he would not do such a thing (2 Samuel 11:11).

David's invitation would have been convenient to accept. Uriah had the king's permission to go home, and the king sent a mess of meat after him. Yet he slept at the door of the king's house with the servants (2 Samuel 11:8-9). His concern reached beyond what he was personally allowed to enjoy. He remembered the men still bearing the burden from which he had briefly been recalled.

Even when David made him drunk, Uriah did not return to his wife (2 Samuel 11:13). The purpose concealed behind the hospitality failed. The servant maintained his course while the king employed his authority to hide a transgression.

David then entrusted him with the letter that ordered his death. Uriah carried it to Joab and returned to the fighting (2 Samuel 11:14-17). The loyalty by which he served his king was used against him. His death did not expose a failure of courage or duty; it exposed the treachery of the command placed over him.

Nathan's charge did not let Uriah disappear into the unnamed losses of battle. The Lord declared that David had killed Uriah with the sword and taken his wife (2 Samuel 12:9). The man whom the king had sought to conceal remained named in the judgment against the king.

The later summary of David's reign again singled out the matter of Uriah the Hittite (1 Kings 15:5). Matthew also identifies Solomon's mother as her who had been the wife of Urias (Matthew 1:6). The record of the royal line did not erase the marriage that David had violated.

Uriah was not delivered from the fatal order. His fidelity must not be measured by whether he escaped suffering. The account honours the servant's conduct while condemning the ruler who exploited it. The throne could command his movements, but it could not make the blood innocent of accusation.

verses.text: And David sent to Joab, saying, Send me Uriah the Hittite. And Joab sent Uriah to David.
And when Uriah was come unto him, David demanded of him how Joab did, and how the people did, and how the war prospered.
And David said to Uriah, Go down to thy house, and wash thy feet. And Uriah departed out of the king’s house, and there followed him a mess of meat from the king.
But Uriah slept at the door of the king’s house with all the servants of his lord, and went not down to his house.
And when they had told David, saying, Uriah went not down unto his house, David said unto Uriah, Camest thou not from thy journey? why then didst thou not go down unto thine house?

And Uriah said unto David, The ark, and Israel, and Judah, abide in tents; and my lord Joab, and the servants of my lord, are encamped in the open fields; shall I then go into mine house, to eat and to drink, and to lie with my wife? as thou livest, and as thy soul liveth, I will not do this thing.

entries.commentary: After the year was expired, at the time when kings go forth to battle, David sent Joab and all Israel to destroy the children of Ammon and besiege Rabbah, but David tarried still at Jerusalem. In the evening he walked upon the roof, saw a woman washing herself who was very beautiful, inquired and learned she was Bathsheba the wife of Uriah the Hittite, sent and took her, and lay with her; and she conceived and told David, I am with child. Masons and people in these fraternities always run here to justify wrongdoing, saying David slept with Bathsheba and the Most High still forgave him. But you are not King David; David was a man like the rest of us, and he messed up, and this is the mess up. About ninety percent of them go right back to David and Bathsheba every time they want to justify some wrongdoing.

David sent to Joab to send him Uriah. When Uriah came, David asked how Joab and the people did and how the war prospered, then told him to go down to his house and wash his feet, sending a mess of meat after him. But Uriah slept at the door of the king's house with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. When David heard it, he asked Uriah why he came not from his journey and went not down. David's plan, which nobody was privy to, was that if Uriah went down and slept with his wife, they could say the child was his. A lot of us do that today: many people raise children that are not theirs, and just because David did it does not make it right.

Uriah told David that the ark and Israel and Judah abode in tents, and Joab and the servants of his lord were encamped in the open fields; so how could he go into his house to eat, drink, and lie with his wife? As David lived, he would not do this thing. David kept him another day and made him drunk, but that evening Uriah still went out to lie on his bed with the servants of his lord and went not down to his house. Uriah had a sense of loyalty that was probably killing David all the more, because David could not deceive this man into laying with his wife. Even drunk, when a man might just go home to sleep it off, Uriah still slept at David's house and would not go down.

In the morning David wrote a letter to Joab and sent it by the hand of Uriah, ordering that Uriah be set in the forefront of the hottest battle and then abandoned, that he might be smitten and die. Joab assigned Uriah to a place where he knew valiant men were, and when the men of the city fought, some of David's servants fell, and Uriah the Hittite died also. David set this man up to get murdered, and Israel does this too, contrary to popular belief. This goes back to Deuteronomy 27: cursed is he that smiteth his neighbour secretly, because nobody knew what David was doing, and cursed is he that taketh reward to slay an innocent person. The reward was that woman; he slew an innocent man who had done nothing.

Joab sent and told David all concerning the war, charging the messenger that if the king's wrath arose over drawing so nigh the city, he should then say that Uriah the Hittite was dead also. When the messenger delivered it, David told him to say to Joab, Let not this thing displease thee, for the sword devoureth one as well as another; make the battle stronger and overthrow the city. Other men of Israel died too, not just Uriah, so with David's sin other men died as well. Joab knew what the king really wanted, so he made sure to name Uriah as dead. David's reply was that it is what it is, the mission was accomplished, you win some and lose some; being content with murder is a wicked thing to do.

When the wife of Uriah heard her husband was dead, she mourned for him, and when the mourning was past, David sent and fetched her to his house and she became his wife and bare him a son. But the thing that David had done displeased the Most High. It displeased the Most High because it was murder; he set the man up to be murdered on a battlefield, which was not a righteous thing. Bathsheba was not innocent either; she was complicit. When David called for her she went, she did not refuse because she was married, and it was consensual, not rape. She knew she was pregnant, so this was deceitful on both sides.

taught.title: 2 Samuel 11: David, Bathsheba, and the Murder of Uriah
